articles.title: A harness inside the app
articles.summary: SHarness gives a process nothing by default. What it needs comes through doors, one job each: the network, the file system, keys, the model, running a command. A policy says which doors are open and how far, and a secret lives behind exactly one of them.
articles.markdown:
*A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. It draws on [SHarness](https://sharness.ai), the owner's design for running agents as small, single-purpose processes that reach the world only through separate, policed doors.*

## The idea

SHarness gives a process nothing by default. What it needs comes through doors, one job each: the network, the file system, keys, the model, running a command. A policy says which doors are open and how far, and a secret lives behind exactly one of them.

An app with a model in it has the same problem at a smaller scale. When the model is asked what to do next, something decides whether it may read a file, open a vault, use a key or reach the network. Today that something is scattered through the code. The brief is to make it explicit, in the same shape:

| Door | What passes through it in the app |
|---|---|
| Network | Every request, to which host, and why |
| File system | Reads and writes, as a virtual file system over notes and vaults |
| Vault | Opening a vault, reading a path, writing a commit |
| Keys | Deriving, signing, encrypting, decrypting: the key never leaves this door |
| Model | Every prompt and every answer, on the device or in Apple's cloud |
| Run | Whatever the app can execute on the model's behalf, if anything |

Each door is a small component with one job, a policy for what it will do, and a record of what it did. This need not be separate processes on iOS; the shape and the records are what matter first.

## Showing it

The reason to build it this way is to be able to watch it. On an iPad or a Mac: the thing being done on the left, the doors on the right, and each request drawn as it passes from one to the other, allowed or refused. The vault engine's "Every step" log is the first, text-only version of this for one door.

As the interface becomes something the model helps decide (see [Two decision engines](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/two-decision-engines/index.html)), this view is how anyone, the developer first, understands why the app did what it did.

## First slice

Not all of it at once. One door first, the model door, with its record and its drawing, used by the first [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) experiment. Then the vault door, which already has its log.

## What is not claimed

Nothing here is a security boundary in SHarness's sense: inside one iOS app there is one process. It is a way to organise and to see, and it says so.

articles.title: A private voice note, and what it would take to use it in a clinic
articles.summary: VoiceDebrief is one example of a pattern that could carry other things than voice notes. A person's own device does the work: it records, a model on the device turns speech into text, and a second model on the device summarises it. Nothing has to leave the device for any of that, so it works...
articles.markdown:
**Kind:** an idea, with corrections. **From:** a conversation recorded in the app on 13 November 2026 between the owner and a clinician, who asked for it to be written down and drawn. Written up by the agent working on the repository, which has also corrected the places where the conversation described the plan as if it were built, or said more than is true.

> This is not legal, regulatory or clinical advice. It says what the software does and does not do, so that the people who are qualified to decide can decide.

*(A picture: A patient's device records, transcribes and summarises a voice note without the internet and encrypts it into a vault. A clinician's QR code gives the patient the clinician's public key; a note sealed to that key crosses a server that cannot read it and is opened on the clinician's device.)*

## The idea in one paragraph

VoiceDebrief is one example of a pattern that could carry other things than voice notes. A person's own device does the work: it records, a model **on the device** turns speech into text, and a second model on the device summarises it. Nothing has to leave the device for any of that, so it works offline. What the person chooses to keep is encrypted on the device into a vault that only their key opens. What they choose to send goes to one other person, encrypted to that person's public key, so that the server carrying it holds bytes it cannot read. There is no account with the company that made the app. The proposal is to try this between a patient and a clinician.

## The workflow, step by step

| Step | What happens | Today |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Speak | The recording is written into the app's own storage as it is spoken | Works |
| 2. Words | Apple's speech model, on the device, produces a transcript with times | Works. English tried; other languages untried |
| 3. Summary | Apple's language model, on the device, writes key points, actions and one sentence | Works, with faults: see below |
| 4. Keep | The note is encrypted on the device into a vault as one signed commit | Works by hand; automatic saving is written, untried |
| 5. Exchange keys | The clinician shows a QR code: their public key and the address of their inbox. The patient scans it once | In build 0.1.9, untried on a device. The receiving side exists as a script, not an app |
| 6. Send | The note is encrypted on the patient's device to the clinician's key and left in their inbox | Works: every note in this project's testing has travelled this way |
| 7. Open | The clinician's device fetches it and opens it with a private key that never left that device | Works, in the script |
| 8. The way back | The clinician writes to the patient, or is given access to part of the patient's vault | Designed, not built |

## What the conversation got right

- **The models run on the device, so it works offline and the audio need not go anywhere.** True of both Apple's speech model and its language model as the app uses them.
- **No login with us.** The app is installed with an Apple ID, which the developer does not see. The developer cannot tell one user from another, and is not meant to.
- **A passkey is unlocked by a face or a finger and kept by Apple so that only your own devices can use it.** True: passkeys live in iCloud Keychain, which is end-to-end encrypted.
- **A vault's key can be taken out and the vault opened in a browser.** True: the vault format is sgit's, and a vault made by the app has been read back that way.
- **The clinician's side is the same design in a different app.** That is the intention: the keys, vaults and inboxes do not change; the screens do.

## What needs correcting

1. **"The model transcribes and separates the speakers."** It transcribes. It does not tell speakers apart: the recording this article came from, with two people talking, came out as one unbroken voice. The app treats every note as one person's memo.
2. **"The passkey is the same one I use for iCloud."** No. A passkey belongs to one site or app. The one used here would be made for this purpose and is separate from the Apple ID. What is shared is where it is kept (iCloud Keychain) and how it is unlocked (Face ID or Touch ID).
3. **"The vault key is made from the passkey."** That is the design, and it already works on the web at pki.sgit.ai. In the app, the arithmetic exists and is tested against published examples, but the sign-in itself is not built. Today the app keeps vault keys in the device's Keychain.
4. **"Because it is on the device and encrypted, it is GDPR compliant."** This is the one to be careful with, and the next section is about it.
5. **"You take a photo of the doctor's QR code and now you have authorised the doctor."** Scanning a code tells the app which key to encrypt to. It does not prove whose key it is. If somebody else's code were shown, the note would go to them, perfectly encrypted.

## On data protection

Doing the work on the device and encrypting before anything leaves it removes a large part of the usual risk: there is no company server holding recordings, no third-party model receiving them, and a breach of the storage server yields ciphertext. Those are real advantages and they are the reason for the design.

They do not make a service "compliant" by themselves. If a clinic used this with patients:

- **Health data is a special category** under the GDPR. Processing it needs a lawful basis and one of the specific conditions for special-category data, whatever the technology.
- **The clinic would be a controller** for what it receives and keeps, with the duties that follow: telling patients what happens to their data, keeping it only as long as needed, answering requests for access and erasure, recording what it does.
- **Encrypted data on a server is still personal data being processed**, and whoever runs that server is acting for somebody. Where it is, and under what contract, still has to be answered. The server not being able to read it is a strong safeguard, not an exemption.
- **A data protection impact assessment** would very probably be expected before use with patients.
- **Losing the key is losing the data.** That is a property of the design. For a clinical record it is also an availability risk that has to be planned for: recovery, and what happens when a patient loses a phone.

The honest summary: this design makes many of the hard questions easier to answer well. It does not answer them for you.

## What a clinic would need that does not exist yet

- **Knowing who a key belongs to.** A register of people and their public keys, where a clinician is verified once by an accountable body and patients' apps check that. The project has this in design (pki.sgit.ai, with delegations that expire), not in the app.
- **The way back.** The patient's own code, so that a clinician can write to a patient, and so that a patient can give a clinician access to one vault and take it away again.
- **Taking access away.** Sending to a key cannot be undone. Shared vaults need keys that can be changed when somebody leaves.
- **A record of who did what.** Every change to a vault is a signed commit, which is a good foundation for an audit trail. Reading is not recorded.
- **Treating the summary as what it is.** In testing, the on-device model has turned a passing remark into a task, mixed up who said what, and misheard names. The audio and the transcript are the record; a summary would need a person to check it before it went anywhere near a clinical note. Whether software that summarises a consultation is regulated as a medical device depends on what it is claimed to do, and is a question for a regulatory specialist.
- **More than one speaker.** A consultation is a conversation.
- **Large files.** A scan is not a voice note. Support for files over 4 MB now exists in the vault engine and is being built into a second app for sharing files.

## A first experiment that would be worth doing

Small, with no real patient data:

1. A clinician and a colleague acting as a patient, each with the app (or the clinician with the receiving script).
2. Exchange codes. The "patient" records three notes of the kind a real one might: a symptom diary entry, a question before an appointment, an account of a week on a new medicine.
3. Look at what arrives, and judge three things: is the transcript good enough to rely on; is the summary safe to show a clinician; how long did the whole thing take, in presses and in seconds.

That would say whether the pattern is worth taking to the people who would have to approve it.

articles.title: People, messages and secrets: the layer under both apps
articles.summary: The idea in one line: every install is a person with keys and an inbox; people meet by exchanging cards; everything they send each other, including secrets, is sealed to the recipient's key and dropped in their inbox. VoiceDebrief and SGit Vaults both stand on it, and so does a secrets manager.
articles.markdown:
**Kind:** an architecture and a brief. **From:** the owner, 14 November 2026: "anybody who installs the app has a public and private key straight away ... register people, kind of like PKI ... identities from the website, and identities shared by QR code, in person or in a WhatsApp message ... a messaging system ... your device becomes the management layer ... a full-blown secrets manager." Written up by the agent working on the repository. Intention, not fact: [what is built](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/built/index.html) says what exists.

The idea in one line: **every install is a person with keys and an inbox; people meet by exchanging cards; everything they send each other, including secrets, is sealed to the recipient's key and dropped in their inbox.** VoiceDebrief and SGit Vaults both stand on it, and so does a secrets manager.

## 1. From the first launch

*(A picture: The first launch makes a key pair for the person, a key for the device, an inbox and a contact card; a secrets store holds access keys and vault keys; pki.sgit.ai is optional.)*

- **Your key pair** (RSA-OAEP 4096 to receive, ECDSA P-256 to sign; the sgit key bundle). Made at first launch, kept in iCloud Keychain so that your other devices have it. *Built in VoiceDebrief (`PKIKit`, the Identity screen); made when asked for, not at first launch; untried on a device.*
- **This device's key**, in the Secure Enclave where there is one, vouched for by your key. *Built in VoiceDebrief; untried.*
- **An inbox**: an append lane on a vault of yours. Anyone holding its link can drop a sealed message in; only your key opens it. *The lane works today (every note sent to the developer goes this way); an inbox per person is not built.*
- **A contact card**: your name, your public keys, your inbox's link, signed by you. Shown as a QR code or a link. *Not built: today's QR code carries an inbox link and one public key, not a signed card.*
- **The secrets store**: access keys, vault keys, passwords and tokens, in the Keychain. Each secret remembers who it was given to. *Not built.*

## 2. Meeting someone

*(A picture: Three ways to exchange cards: in person by QR code, by a message such as WhatsApp, or from the register. Each contact keeps how it was met.)*

| Way | How | How far to trust it |
|---|---|---|
| In person | Each scans the other's QR code | The most: you saw the person and the code together |
| By a message | The card as a QR picture or a link, on WhatsApp, Signal, email | As far as the channel it came by |
| From the register | Look up a name or fingerprint at pki.sgit.ai | As far as the register's checks on that person |

A contact keeps how it was met, and can be checked later (fingerprints compared face to face, or the register vouching). Adding is **two-way**: when you add someone, the app offers to send them your card, so they can write back. Agents are contacts like any other: a Claude session has a card and an inbox (`tools/conductor/` makes them).

## 3. Messages and secrets

*(A picture: A message or a secret is sealed on the sender's device to the recipient's key, dropped in their inbox, and opened on their device, which checks for new messages on opening, every minute while in use, and less often when idle.)*

A message is sealed to the recipient's public key and signed with the sender's, on the sender's device (the envelope `PKIKit` already makes). It can carry text, a voice note (what VoiceDebrief sends today), **a secret**, a vault invitation, or a card.

**Checking for new messages.** There are no push events, so the app asks: when it opens or comes to the front, every minute while it is in use, and less and less often when idle (the owner's pattern from the website). One list call on one inbox per check: little traffic.

## 4. The secrets manager

The owner's point: there is a gap in the market, because sharing a secret safely is still awkward. Here it is one gesture: pick the secret, pick the contact, send. What it needs:

- **Kinds**: a server access key, a vault key, a password, an API token, a note.
- **Kept** in the Keychain (iCloud Keychain by default, a switch for this device only), with a backup in one of your vaults if you choose.
- **Shared** as a sealed message to a contact; **received** into the store with one tap.
- **Remembered**: who holds each secret and since when, so that a secret can be changed and the new value sent to everyone who should have it, and nobody who should not.
- **Shown** only after Face ID or the passcode, copied with an expiry on the clipboard.

## 5. The access key, and the first message

A person needs the server access key to write to a vault server, including to create their own inbox. The owner's assumption: everyone who uses the app is given it. That makes it the first secret most people will receive, which raises a chicken-and-egg question: how does it arrive before they have an inbox?

The answer this design proposes: **the first exchange carries it.** The newcomer shows their card (their public key, no inbox yet); whoever invites them seals the access key to that key and sends it back by the same route, a QR code or a WhatsApp message. A sealed secret is safe on WhatsApp: only the newcomer's key opens it. With the access key in their store, the newcomer's app creates their inbox and sends their full card. This also settles issue 110 for SGit Vaults: a teammate receives the access key as a secret, held and remembered like any other.

## Where it is built

One Swift package shared by both apps (proposed name `SGitPeople`): the key bundle (moving `PKIKit` out of VoiceDebrief), contact cards, contacts, inboxes and the check for new messages, the message format, and the secrets store. Each app adds its own screens. A dedicated session builds it.

## Decisions for the owner

1. **Access key distribution** as in section 5, or each person brings their own.
2. **The card's format**: a new signed card, compatible with pki.sgit.ai's key bundle (proposed), shown as a QR code and a link.
3. **Where inboxes live**: on each person's own vault (proposed), or one shared vault for a team.
4. **The register**: publishing to pki.sgit.ai optional and off by default (proposed).

articles.title: Synthetic users
articles.summary: The app is built by an agent that cannot see it. Continuous integration compiles and tests it; the owner sees it on a device. Between the two there is nobody checking whether a person arriving for the first time can find the record button, understand what a vault is, or get back from the place a tap...
articles.markdown:
*A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

## The problem

The app is built by an agent that cannot see it. Continuous integration compiles and tests it; the owner sees it on a device. Between the two there is nobody checking whether a person arriving for the first time can find the record button, understand what a vault is, or get back from the place a tap took them.

## The idea

Invented users, each with a purpose and a level of knowledge, who walk the screens and report where they hesitated, guessed wrong or got lost. The newsroom at sgit.ai does this for a website, one screenshot at a time. The same applies here.

For example:

- someone who wants to record a memo while driving and has never heard of a vault;
- someone careful about privacy who wants to know exactly what leaves the phone;
- a developer who wants to see every request the app makes;
- someone who lost a recording in another app and does not trust this one.

## How it would work

1. **Pictures of every screen.** A workflow in continuous integration runs the app in a simulator, one launch per screen with sample data, and keeps a screenshot of each on an iPhone and an iPad. The sibling repository has this already; it is to be carried over. It also gives the agent its first sight of its own work.
2. **A walk.** A synthetic user is given a task and the screenshots, and says at each step what it would tap and what it expects. Where its expectation and the next screen disagree is a finding.
3. **A record.** Findings are kept as files, each with the screen, the user and what went wrong, and a status as review findings have elsewhere in this family.

## Limits

A synthetic user reads a picture. It does not feel a button that is too small for a thumb, hear nothing, or drive a car. Simulators have no speech model and no Apple Intelligence, so screens that depend on them are shown with sample data. The owner on a device remains the test that counts.

articles.title: The lab
articles.summary: VoiceDebrief for iOS started as one job: a voice note in, a transcript and a debrief out. In a day it gained on-device speech, an on-device model, vaults, signed commits and encrypted lanes, and it runs as one app on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, delivered by TestFlight. That combination is rarer...
articles.markdown:
*A brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent. Nothing here is built unless [what is built](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/built/index.html) says so.*

## The idea

VoiceDebrief for iOS started as one job: a voice note in, a transcript and a debrief out. In a day it gained on-device speech, an on-device model, vaults, signed commits and encrypted lanes, and it runs as one app on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, delivered by TestFlight. That combination is rarer than the product it was built for.

So for now the app is also a laboratory. The product that ships will be smaller and more focused. The lab exists to get the primitives and the key workflows right, and to find out what is possible, before deciding what that product is.

Because nothing here is being submitted to the App Store yet, the lab can ask for any capability Apple offers.

## What it should explore

| | Experiment | Question |
|---|---|---|
| L01 | One prompt, tools on and off | What does the on-device model do with a single tightly scoped prompt and a chosen set of tools? How reliable are its tool calls? |
| L02 | The model drives the screen | Can the model choose what the interface shows next, through function calls, from a state the code hands it? |
| L03 | The model edits a page | Can it write or change an HTML or JSON page in a vault that the app then renders? |
| L04 | Apple's larger model | The same prompts on Private Cloud Compute: what does 32,768 tokens and reasoning buy? |
| L05 | Another provider through the same framework | iOS 27 lets a session run on other models, Claude among them. What changes, and what does it cost in privacy? |
| L06 | Images | What can Image Playground and image input do for a note: a cover, a photographed whiteboard? |
| L07 | A file system for the model | A virtual file system over a vault, with access granted folder by folder |
| L08 | Graphs from notes | Semantic graphs from transcripts, linked across notes and vaults |
| L09 | Code inside the app | Can anything like a script run natively and safely on the device? |
| L10 | Many ways to show the same thing | Several interfaces for one workflow, compared on the three devices |

Each experiment is a screen in a Lab section of the app, with what was asked, what came back, how long it took and what it cost shown plainly. An experiment that fails is a result.

## Rules

- An experiment says what it is. Nothing in the lab is presented as a finished feature.
- Everything the model is given and everything it returns can be seen. See [Two decision engines](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/two-decision-engines/index.html).
- What works is rebuilt properly, and probably moved out into its own app or package. The lab is where it is found, not where it lives.

articles.title: The vault is a version-controlled store
articles.summary: A vault is usually described by its encryption. That undersells it. A vault is a version-controlled data store: files, history, branches, signed commits. The encryption is one property; the history is another, and for an ordinary application it may be the more useful one. Anything an app keeps could...
articles.markdown:
*A position and a brief. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

## The position

A vault is usually described by its encryption. That undersells it. A vault is a version-controlled data store: files, history, branches, signed commits. The encryption is one property; the history is another, and for an ordinary application it may be the more useful one. Anything an app keeps could be kept this way and gain history, integrity and a way to move.

And a vault is a good way to move data. Two devices, two people or a person and an agent can exchange work by exchanging vaults, or by writing to each other's lanes.

## The correction

The first vault screen in this app asks for an SG/Send access token before it will create a vault. That is wrong in principle. **Creating a vault needs no server and no token.** A vault can exist on the device alone. A token is needed only to push it to a server, and the server itself should be something you configure, not something assumed.

So:

- **A vault is local first.** Create, commit, read and browse with no network.
- **A server is a remote.** Add one, with its address and its token, when you want the vault elsewhere. Push and pull are explicit.
- **Some things need a remote.** A lane, where others write to you, lives on a server. That is one use, not the definition.

## The brief

| | What |
|---|---|
| Local vaults | Create and use a vault on the device with no token. The engine already writes to a folder in its tests; the app should use that |
| Remotes | A list of servers, each with an address and a token in the Keychain. A vault may have none, one or several |
| Several vaults, several lanes | Register them with names. Choose where a note goes: one vault, several, a lane to a person or to an agent that conducts other agents |
| A file system | The vault as a virtual file system the app, and later the model, can be given in part: this folder, read only |
| Vault apps | A vault can hold an app: pages and data rendered from the vault. Render them here. Then create and edit them here, and see whether the model can |
| Graphs | Every note processed into the store, then linked: semantic graphs across notes and across vaults |

## Order

Local vaults and remotes first, because they correct something that is wrong today. Then several named vaults and lanes, which the recording workflow needs. The file system, vault apps and graphs are [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) work.

articles.title: Two decision engines
articles.summary: An application used to have one thing that decided what happens next: its code. With a model on the device it has two. The code decides by rules somebody wrote. The model decides by judgement nobody wrote. The interesting question is not which is better. It is how the two are joined.
articles.markdown:
*A position. From the owner's voice memo of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

An application used to have one thing that decided what happens next: its code. With a model on the device it has two. The code decides by rules somebody wrote. The model decides by judgement nobody wrote. The interesting question is not which is better. It is how the two are joined.

## The position

**The code owns the states. The model is asked one question at a time.**

The application is a set of states and the moves between them: a state machine, as the pipeline already is. At a given state the code may hand the model a small, exact package (this state, this data, these tools) and ask one of two things:

- **What should happen next?** The model answers by calling a function the code offered.
- **Say this another way.** The model turns one form into another: a transcript into a debrief, a debrief into a title, a request into a query. A translation or a projection, not a conversation.

There is no long history. Each prompt stands alone, built for that state, as small as it can be. That is what makes it cheap enough for an on-device model with a few thousand tokens of context, and it is what makes it inspectable: for any decision the model made, the whole of what it was shown fits on one screen.

## Why this shape

- **Control.** The model can only do what the functions offered at that state allow. A tool that is not offered does not exist for it.
- **Debugging.** A one-prompt decision can be replayed. A decision buried in a long conversation cannot.
- **Size.** Small models are good at small, literal tasks and poor at long ones. This asks them only for the first kind.
- **Privacy.** What leaves the code for the model is chosen each time, and can be shown each time.

## Where it leads

If the model can choose the next step through function calls, it can choose what the interface shows. The screens stop being fixed pages and become what the code and the model agree to show for this state: intelligence in the application, not beside it. That only works if every decision can be seen, replayed and overruled, which is why the [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) and the [harness](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/a-harness-inside-the-app/index.html) come first.

## What is not claimed

None of this is built. Whether Apple's on-device model calls tools reliably enough to drive anything is the first experiment, not an assumption.

articles.title: Voice everywhere
articles.summary: Losing a voice memo is the worst thing this app can do. A person who spoke for ten minutes while walking will not say it again the same way. Everything else can fail and be retried: the transcript, the debrief, the vault, the lane. The recording cannot.
articles.markdown:
*An idea. From the owner's voice memos of 13 November 2026, written up by the agent.*

## Never lose a recording

Losing a voice memo is the worst thing this app can do. A person who spoke for ten minutes while walking will not say it again the same way. Everything else can fail and be retried: the transcript, the debrief, the vault, the lane. The recording cannot.

This is why the screen shows the words and the level as you speak. It is not decoration. It is the evidence that the recording is being heard and kept, and it is what lets someone trust the app enough to stop checking it.

It is also why the note exists before the first word and why the recording is kept in a form that survives the app dying. See [the design](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/design/index.html), where capture without loss is the first job.

## Voice as the way in

Recording should not be a place you go to. It should be available from wherever you are: one control, on every screen, that starts a voice memo and returns you to what you were doing. The memo then goes where it should: the library, a vault, a lane to someone else.

The workflow that matters most: speaking while driving or walking, hands and eyes elsewhere, and trusting that it was captured; then, later, giving that memo to a particular person or agent.

## More than one way to show it

There is no reason to pick one interface before trying several. One of them might look less like a recorder and more like an assistant that is listening: a single visual that shows it hears you, in the manner of the assistants in films. The [lab](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/articles/the-lab/index.html) is where these are compared, on the phone, the tablet and the laptop.

## What is built

Recording with the words and the level as you speak, and a note that exists from the start. Not built: a control on every screen, starting from the Action button or Siri, the other interfaces. Recording with the screen locked is declared and untested.

A passkey, behind Face ID, proves it is you. iCloud Keychain carries your secrets to your other devices, encrypted so that Apple cannot read them. Vaults hold the data, encrypted and version controlled, on a store that sees only ciphertext. Put together: sign in to the same Apple account on a new device, authenticate, the vault keys arrive, the app pulls the vaults, and the same files are there. The vault provides the synchronisation, and when two devices write at once it behaves as git does: the first wins, the second pulls, merges and pushes.

## Four keys, four homes

| Key | What it is for | Must it travel? | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vault keys, server tokens | Open and write vaults | Yes | iCloud Keychain, synchronised. **On by default** (owner's decision), with a switch to keep them on this device only |
| The user's key pair | Who you are: signs as you, lets others encrypt to you | Yes | iCloud Keychain to begin with; the master vault, opened by the passkey, when that is built. Never the Secure Enclave, which cannot let a key out and cannot hold an RSA key |
| The device's key pair | Which device, or which install of the app, did this | Never | The Secure Enclave of that device where it can be, otherwise the Keychain marked for this device only. Meant to be lost with the device or the app |
| Public halves | Checking the above | Freely | In the vault beside the data. The user's also in a register such as pki.sgit.ai |

Two details that follow:

- **A synchronised Keychain item cannot also demand Face ID.** That protection exists only for items that stay on one device. It is the main reason the passkey and master vault remain the end state: the passkey is behind Face ID every time, and the keys sit inside a vault rather than loose in the Keychain.
- **Keychain items survive deleting an app.** For the device key to die with the app, the app has to wipe it the first time it runs after a reinstall.

## Linking the device to the person

Every commit is already signed by a device key whose public half is in the vault. What is missing is anything that says whose device it is. The addition is a short statement in the vault, signed by the user's key: this device key is mine, from this date, for these uses. A reader then checks two things: the device signed the commit, and the person vouched for the device. Losing a device means withdrawing one statement and nothing else.

## Optionally, a person in the register

The app must work with no register at all. As an option, the owner can connect it to the identity he already has at [pki.sgit.ai](https://pki.sgit.ai), where his key pair is kept behind a passkey.

That site already has the flow, "Sign in with pki.sgit.ai", with no server in between:

1. The app makes a key pair and sends the person to `pki.sgit.ai/authorize/` with a request naming the app's public key, what it wants to do and for how long.
2. There, signed in with their passkey, the person reads who is asking and signs a delegation with their own key: this key acts for me at this site, for these uses, until this date.
3. The delegation comes back to the app, which keeps it and attaches it to what it signs.
4. Anyone can then check, against the register and starting from a root they trust, that the note was signed by a key a registered person vouched for. Withdrawing the link in the register ends it.

So without the extra step the app proves "the same device signed all of these". With it, the app proves "a person in the public register stands behind this device".

One thing to settle when building: that flow returns its answer to a web address on the asking site, so the app needs a page on its own site that hands the answer back to the app.

articles.title: The sgit app: design for milestone one
articles.summary: sgit as a native app for iPhone, iPad and Mac: vaults, files and commits, with the same encrypted format as the sgit command and the web Vault UI. This page is intention. What is built says how much of it exists. It lives in this repository for now, beside VoiceDebrief for iOS, and shares its vault...
articles.markdown:
sgit as a native app for iPhone, iPad and Mac: vaults, files and commits, with the same encrypted format as the `sgit` command and the web Vault UI. This page is intention. [What is built](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/sgit-app/built/index.html) says how much of it exists. It lives in this repository for now, beside VoiceDebrief for iOS, and shares its vault engine; it will move to a repository of its own.

## Why it starts here

The owner's words, 13 November 2026: the team needs to share photos, videos and large files, and "at the moment there isn't an easy way to do it". So the first milestone is narrow: a person picks photos, videos or any files on a phone, they go into a vault, and a teammate can open them. Managing vaults and commits grows from there towards what the web Vault UI does.

## The jobs, in order

1. **Put files in a vault without losing them.** A selection is copied into the app before anything else happens. From then on a failed upload, a closed app or a lost connection can be taken up again.
2. **Find and open what is in a vault.** Folders, thumbnails, a full-size view, a video player.
3. **Give the vault to somebody**, knowing what that gives them.
4. **See what happened.** Every commit, which key signed it, what it changed.

## What was read first

| Source | What it settled |
|---|---|
| `sgit-ai` 0.27.0 (the Python package) | The format and the protocol. A blob over 4 MB encrypted is uploaded in parts of 10 MB to URLs the server signs, flagged `large` in its tree entry, and read back from a signed URL in ranges of 8 MB |
| The web Vault UI: its JavaScript as served at vault.sgraph.ai, read by this session; its source (the Send repository at commit `da293d4`, 18 October 2026), read by the parent session | The features and the words. It encrypts each file whole and sends it in a batch, and refuses a write over 3 MB from a vault app; its own source says a large upload through signed URLs "is not yet supported". It does read large files through a signed URL. Its library can move a branch with compare-and-swap (`pushIfMatch`), but its screens use the unconditional `push`, which the source notes can drop somebody else's commits |
| The server's published API description | Reading needs no access token, including the signed URL for a large object. Writing needs the access token and the vault's write key |
| The live server, with `sgit` itself | The exchange for a large object works on `dev.send.sgraph.ai` as the package describes it (a throwaway vault, destroyed afterwards) |

Both source repositories were read on 14 November 2026, once the owner asked for them to be cloned. From the web Vault's source: it opens a vault this app made from its vault key, without writing anything, and shows it as "Untitled Vault" because the app writes no settings file; its link is the site's root followed by `#` and the key; it chooses the signed URL for a file by size, not by the `large` flag; its own commits are unsigned, which the app's history shows as "Not signed"; and when it rewrites a folder it drops the `large` flag and the file types, which the app tolerates by going by size too. None of that has been tried between the two yet.

## Decisions

| | Decision |
|---|---|
| One selection, one commit | Everything picked together becomes one signed commit on the branch `current`, with the message the web Vault UI writes: `Add IMG_0001.HEIC`, or `Add 3 files: a, b, c` |
| Staging | A picked file is copied into the app, then encrypted to disk under its object id, then uploaded, then named in the commit. Each step is recorded, so a retry sends only what the server lacks |
| A refused push | If somebody else committed first the server refuses the move (compare-and-swap). Adding files needs no merge: the same staged files are committed again on the new head, automatically |
| Large files | Encrypted and decrypted from disk to disk, a megabyte at a time. Uploaded in parts, three at a time; downloaded in ranges, three at a time. See "Limits" |
| Where a file goes | Into the folder that is open, under its own name. A name already taken gets a number |
| Reading | A file is fetched and decrypted when it is opened. The decrypted copy is in the app's cache folder only, which the system may empty, and which Settings can empty |
| Where a vault lives | A vault you create is made and kept on this device: no account, no token, no network, and it takes files at once. It goes to a server when you choose to share it, which is the first time an access token is asked for, with the reason. From then on the server is where it lives and this device reads and writes it there, as it does a vault added by its key. One server (`dev.send.sgraph.ai`) for now |
| Keys | Vault keys, the access token and the device's commit-signing key are in this app's Keychain, on this device only. This app does not share a Keychain with VoiceDebrief |
| Honesty | No screen says a file is in the vault before the commit that names it has been pushed and read back |

## The words

The owner's and sgit's: **vault**, **vault key** (reads and writes), **read key** (reads only), **access key** (the server's own word is access token), **commit**, **history**, **branch**. The app says **Add** for putting files in, **Refresh** for fetching the latest, and **Send to the server** for the one push a vault made on the device needs.

## The screens

**Vaults.** The vaults this device knows. Add one by pasting its key or scanning a QR code; create one. Each row says whether the key can write.

**A vault.** The folder that is open: folders first, then files, as a grid of thumbnails or a list. On an iPad or a Mac the folders are also a tree down the left, as in the web Vault. Files and folders can be dropped on it from the desktop, and a file can be dragged out. Add (from Photos, from Files), New folder by naming one when adding, Refresh, Share, History. Uploads in progress sit at the top with a bar for each file and one for the whole selection, and a failed one says why and offers Try again and Discard.

**A file.** An image at full size with zoom; a video in the system player; anything else in Quick Look. Save to Photos and Share. Delete and rename are a commit each.

**Share.** The vault key as text and as a QR code, under a plain statement: whoever holds it can read everything, add, change and delete, and it cannot be taken back. Below it the read key, for somebody who should only look. See "Giving somebody the vault".

**History.** The commits, newest first: the message, the time, the short id, the fingerprint of the key that signed it and whether the signature verified, and whether that key is this device's. A commit opens to the files it added, changed and removed.

**Settings.** The server and the access token; this device's signing key (its fingerprint); the cache and a button to empty it; every step the vault engine has taken; the version.

## Giving somebody the vault

What exists today, and what each gives:

| Mechanism | Where it exists | What the other person gets |
|---|---|---|
| The vault key, `passphrase:vault id` | sgit, the web UI, this app | Everything, for ever: read, write, delete. It cannot be revoked; the only remedy is a new vault |
| The same key as a link, `vault.sgraph.ai/#key` | The web UI | The same, opened in a browser with nothing to install |
| A read key, `sgit_private_read_…` | sgit and this app's engine. The web UI shows it but cannot yet open with it | Read only, live, for ever. Cannot be revoked |
| A read-only token, `ro-word-word-1234` | The web UI's token manager, marked there as a test harness | Read only, live, with an expiry and a way to revoke it. The token unlocks a small encrypted record on the server that holds the read key |
| `sgit publish` | sgit | A static, read-only copy for a website |

There is no snapshot share: nothing gives "these files as they are now and nothing later".

**Proposal.** Milestone one ships the first three, because they need nothing new on any side: the key as text and QR, the web link, and the read key. For a team sharing photos that is enough, and the warning is on the screen. The right next step is the read-only token, because it is the only one that can be taken back, but it should be built once: the web UI's version is a test harness, and the app, sgit and the web UI should agree on one format first. That is a question for the owner, and is issue 104.

## Limits, stated plainly

- **The format encrypts a file as one AES-GCM message.** sgit and the web UI therefore hold a whole file, and its whole ciphertext, in memory. The app does not: it computes the same bytes as a stream. Its limit is free space on the device (the staged copy and the ciphertext exist together until the upload ends, so about twice the file), and AES-GCM's own limit of about 64 GB a message.
- **What could not be avoided.** Each upload part is held in memory while it is sent: three parts of 10 MB. A blob that sgit deflated and that is over 4 MB is inflated in memory, up to 64 MB. A server without signed URLs (a self-hosted one) takes a large object in one request, which the app allows up to 64 MB. Thumbnails are made from the full image, so a folder of photographs is fetched whole the first time it is shown.
- **The other end.** A teammate opening a large video in the web UI needs it to fit in the browser's memory; `sgit clone` on a computer needs it to fit in memory once.
- **A vault on this device only is on this device only.** Until it is sent to a server there is one copy. Forgetting it deletes it, and the app says so before it does.
- **An upload stops when the app is suspended.** It is taken up again when the app returns: parts already sent in an unfinished object are sent again, finished objects are not. Background uploads are after milestone one.
- **A vault with packs** (objects stored as zips) is refused, as it is by the engine today.

## Milestone one

1. Add a vault by key or QR code; create one.
2. Add photos, videos and files; progress for each and overall; retry and discard; nothing picked is lost.
3. Files over 4 MB, written and read, checked against sgit in both directions by CI.
4. Browse: folders, thumbnails, full size, video, Quick Look, Save to Photos, Share.
5. Share the vault: key, QR code, web link, read key, with the warning.
6. History: commits, signer, what changed.

## After it, in this order

1. A vault that stays on the device after it is shared, with push and pull and a choice of servers, as VoiceDebrief has since issue 011. That needs two things first: a merge for when two people add at once (today the app commits straight to the server, where a refused push is simply tried again), and a way to keep a vault's trees on the device without fetching every video in it. Then keys in iCloud Keychain (017).
2. A share extension: "send to vault" from Photos and Files.
3. Background uploads.
4. A file-level merge for edits and deletions that collide (adding already needs none).
5. Branches: list, switch, create.
6. A read-only token that can be revoked, once its format is agreed.

articles.title: A secrets manager made of people and vaults
articles.summary: The design for the secrets manager in SGit Vaults, asked for by the owner on 14 November 2026. This page is intention. Built so far, compiled and tested but not yet used on a device: questions for the owner, the first secrets screens and the keys in iCloud Keychain (steps 1 to 3 below), described in...
articles.markdown:
The design for the secrets manager in SGit Vaults, asked for by the owner on 14 November 2026. **This page is intention.** Built so far, compiled and tested but not yet used on a device: questions for the owner, the first secrets screens and the keys in iCloud Keychain (steps 1 to 3 below), described in the reality file. What is built is in [the reality file](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/sgit-app/built/index.html), and this page will say plainly as each part arrives.

The owner's words: "a full-blown secrets manager ... passwords, secrets, passkeys", "the synchronisation between devices ... has to be completely transparent", "the collaboration of secrets between people", "how do we go from one person to two people, three, five, the whole group, where each one trusts the other", "a visual representation of the trust", "every team can do this independently", "it is also going to be the foundation for things like the CRM vault".

Earlier experiments it builds on: [secrets.sgit.ai](https://secrets.sgit.ai/) (a zero-knowledge secrets manager in the browser, designed, not built) and [pki.sgit.ai](https://pki.sgit.ai/) (people, their keys, and links that count only when both sides confirm them).

## The idea in one drawing

```
            you                         your team
   ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │  iPhone  iPad  Mac│        │  Ana   Ben   Chloe  Dev  │
   │     \     |    /  │        │    \    |     |    /     │
   │   one key bundle  │◀──────▶│   cards swapped, both    │
   │   one inbox       │ trust  │   ways confirmed         │
   └────────┬─────────┘        └────────────┬─────────────┘
            │ opens                          │ opens
            ▼                                ▼
   ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │  "My secrets"     │        │  "Team: devices"          │
   │   a vault         │        │   a vault, its key sealed │
   │   secrets/*.json  │        │   to each member          │
   └──────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘
            ▲                                ▲
            └──────── the same app, the same format ───────┘
                 a secret is a file in a vault; a team is
                 the people a vault's key was sealed to
```

Two things carry the whole design:

1. **A secret is a file in a vault.** One encrypted JSON file per entry, in the vault's `secrets/` folder. So everything vaults already do comes free: history of every change, signed by who made it; sync with no conflicts between different entries; the web Vault and the `sgit` command can read it; a vault on the device first and on a server when you choose.
2. **A team is the people a vault's key was sealed to.** No company account, no admin, no server of ours. Five people who have swapped cards can make a shared vault in one step, and anything in it is shared. A "CRM vault" later is the same thing with different files in it.

## What makes it different

Ordinary password managers keep your secrets in their company's cloud, behind an account they run, and sharing goes through their servers and their idea of a "team". This one has:

- **No account.** Nobody signs up for anything. A person is a key pair made on their own device.
- **No company in the middle.** The vault server stores ciphertext it cannot read; it never sees a name or a password.
- **Trust you can see.** A map of who has confirmed whom, built from both people's own word. Nobody can add themselves to your team.
- **History of every secret.** Who changed the Wi-Fi password, and when, signed by their device.
- **Secrets that can be given safely.** Sealed to one person's key; a photograph of the screen gives nothing away.
- **Agents are people too.** An AI session has a key and an inbox, and can be given exactly one secret, with a record that it was.
- **Nothing to export.** The format is open and the files are yours; the `sgit` command reads them on any computer.

### What the research says

[The field and the opportunity](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/sgit-app/secrets/opportunity/index.html) is a research brief on eleven managers and secret tools. Its points that change this design:

- **Every major manager's sharing trusts its own server to hand over the other person's public key.** A 2026 ETH Zurich study found more than 25 attacks on Bitwarden, LastPass and Dashlane by a dishonest server, sharing among them. Here the key comes from a card confirmed in person, never from the server. That is the strongest case for the in-person step, so the app should make it quick, not skip it.
- **Small-team sharing is where the others are weakest**: free plans stop at two people, and Apple's shared groups have no roles. A team of five with no admin and no account is the opening.
- **Agents leak secrets at scale** (about 28.65 million new secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025). Giving an agent one sealed secret, with a record, is a feature nobody has.
- **Removing someone** means a new vault key *and* changing what they saw. The app must say so, and offer a checklist.
- **Recovery** is where people give up and where security weakens. Proposed later: three of five people you trust each hold a sealed part.

Ten things this design could do better than all of them are ranked in the brief, each with its risk.

## From one person to a team

```
  1. alone          2. two people          3. three           5. the team
  ───────────       ──────────────         ──────────         ─────────────
     (you)           (you)═══(Ana)          (you)═══(Ana)       (you)══(Ana)
                                              ║     ╱            ║ ╲  ╱ ║
  a key bundle,     met in person:            ║   ╱             ║  ╳   ║
  made on this      scan each other's        (Ben)              ║ ╱  ╲ ║
  device; "My       cards, take a photo,                       (Ben)══(Chloe)
  secrets" vault    both confirm             Ana and Ben           ╲  ╱
  on this device                             confirm each           (Dev)
                    ═══ a link both          other too, or
                        people confirmed     only through you  a shared vault
                    ─── one side only                          for all five
```

**1. Alone.** The app makes a key bundle the first time it is needed, not at first launch. "My secrets" is a vault on this device. Nothing needs a network or an account.

**2. Two people, in person.** Each shows their card as a QR code; the other scans it. The app asks for a photo of the person in front of you (kept on your device) and what to call them. Each confirms. A link counts only when both have confirmed: one side alone is drawn dashed, as "waiting for Ana".

**2b. Two people, apart.** The card goes by WhatsApp, Signal or mail as a link. It is a weaker way of meeting, and the map says so ("met by message"), until you confirm the fingerprint on a call: four groups of four characters, read aloud.

**3 to 5. A group.** Each new person meets whoever is nearest. Ben, who has met only you, sees Ana as "known to someone you trust" and can meet her directly later. The map shows the links that exist; the app suggests the ones that are missing ("Ben and Chloe have not confirmed each other").

**The team's vault.** "Make a shared vault for these people": pick them on the map, name it ("Team: devices"), and the vault's key is sealed to each person's key and dropped in their inbox. Each of them sees it arrive and opens it with one tap. From then on, a password added by any of them is there for all of them, with who added it.

## The trust map

```
                       ┌───────┐
              ┌────────│  you  │────────┐
              │        └───┬───┘        │
           in person    in person    by message
              │            │         (dashed until
          ┌───┴───┐    ┌───┴───┐      confirmed)
          │  Ana  │════│  Ben  │    ┌ ─ ─ ─ ┐
          └───┬───┘    └───────┘      Chloe
              │                     └ ─ ─ ─ ┘
           in person
          ┌───┴───┐
          │  Dev  │   ◀ known to Ana, not yet to you
          └───────┘
```

Each person is drawn with their photo. A solid line is a link both people confirmed; dashed is one side only. A line says how they met. Tapping a person shows their fingerprint, when you met, the vaults you share and the secrets you gave each other. An agent is drawn as a robot face instead of a photo.

The map is computed on your device from what you know: your own contacts and the shared vaults' member lists. It is never published anywhere unless you choose to (pki.sgit.ai's register is optional, and off).

## A secret

```
  secrets/2026-11-14-office-wifi.json   (encrypted in the vault, as every file)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ kind      wifi                               │
  │ name      Office Wi-Fi                        │
  │ fields    network: SGit-Office                │
  │           password: ••••••••••••             │
  │ note      the router is in the cupboard       │
  │ tags      office                              │
  │ changed   14 Nov 2026, by Ana (iPad)  ✓signed │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Kinds, each with the fields it needs: **login** (site, username, password, one-time code), **device** (a laptop, tablet or phone and its passcode: the owner's first use), **Wi-Fi**, **card**, **note**, **token** (API keys), **vault key** and **read key** (opens the vault in one tap), **server access key**, **recovery code**. Values are shown only after Face ID, are copied to the clipboard for two minutes and never leave this device, and are hidden in the app switcher.

**Passkeys.** iOS lets a third-party app keep and use passwords and passkeys in other apps and in Safari only as an **AutoFill credential provider**, an extension that needs a capability switched on for the app in Apple's developer portal. Until then the app records which passkeys exist and where, without holding them. The owner's step is in the list at the end.

## Sync, without thinking about it

```
     iPhone                      iPad                       Mac
  ┌──────────┐               ┌──────────┐              ┌──────────┐
  │ vault    │◀── iCloud ───▶│ vault    │◀── iCloud ──▶│ vault    │
  │ keys     │   Keychain    │ keys     │   Keychain   │ keys     │
  └────┬─────┘               └────┬─────┘              └────┬─────┘
       │  push / pull             │                          │
       └──────────────▶  vault server (ciphertext)  ◀────────┘
```

Your vault keys live in iCloud Keychain, so every device signed into your Apple account opens the same vaults with no setup. The vaults themselves sync through the vault server: the app pulls when it opens and when it comes to the front, and pushes after every change. Two devices changing different secrets never conflict, because each secret is its own file; two changing the same secret at once keep both and ask which is right.

Writing to the server needs an access key; the owner will connect payment for that. Until a person has one, "My secrets" stays on the device it was made on, and the app says so.

## Messages and questions

People talk through their inboxes: a sealed note, a card, a secret, a vault invitation. The same channel is how the app can ask **its owner** questions while it is being built: a Questions screen where a question waits, and the answer can be typed or spoken with the keyboard's dictation, and goes to the developers sealed to their key.

## What is built in which order

| Step | What | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Questions for the owner, answered by typing or dictation | nothing new |
| 2 | Secrets: entries in a vault's `secrets/` folder, the kinds above, Face ID, copy, history | nothing new |
| 3 | Vault keys in iCloud Keychain, pull on open, push on change | an access key for the server part |
| 4 | People: card, scan, photo, two-way confirmation (the people session's screens) | SGitPeople |
| 5 | The trust map | step 4 |
| 6 | A shared vault for chosen people, sealed to each | step 4 and an inbox each |
| 7 | AutoFill: passwords and passkeys in Safari and other apps | the owner switches on the capability |

## For the owner

Questions are also in the app (Settings, Questions) once step 1 is built.

1. **Where "My secrets" lives.** Proposed: a vault like any other (on the device first, on the server once there is an access key). The alternative is iCloud Keychain only, which syncs for free but cannot be shared or read by the `sgit` command.
2. **Photos of people.** Proposed: kept on your device only; not in the card, so a card stays small enough for one QR code.
3. **AutoFill and passkeys.** Needs "AutoFill Credential Provider" switched on for `ai.sgit.vaults.app` in the Apple developer portal, and an App Group. Shall I prepare it?
4. **Recovery.** If all your devices are lost, the vault keys go with iCloud Keychain. Proposed for later: a printed recovery sheet, or a second person who holds a sealed copy.
5. **What a member of a shared vault can do.** Today, everything (they hold the vault key). Read-only members are possible with a read key; "may add, may not delete" needs the server.

## Ideas

- **A team with no admin and no account** **(proposed)**: five people swap cards and confirm each other, then share a vault, with no sign-up, invoice or IT person.
- **Sharing a server cannot redirect** **(proposed)**: the key a secret is sealed to comes from a card confirmed in person, never from the server, which shuts out the key-swapping attacks found in other managers in 2026.
- **One secret for one agent** **(proposed)**: give an AI session exactly one API key, sealed to its key, with a record of when and to whom.
- **Signed history of every secret** **(proposed)**: who changed the router password and when, signed by their device, with the earlier version one tap away.
- **Ask someone outside the team for a secret** **(proposed)**: a contractor drops the Wi-Fi or a server key into your inbox; they get no way to read anything back.
- **Rotation on a branch** **(proposed)**: change a key, test it, then merge, so the team is never half on the old one and half on the new.
- **Recovery through people you trust** **(proposed)**: lose every device and get back in with three of five people each holding a sealed part; no company reset.
- **Leaving someone out, honestly** **(proposed)**: removing a member makes a new vault key and shows the checklist of secrets they saw, with a change action for each.
- **A spotted secret** **(proposed)**: Apple's on-device model notices a key pasted into a note or a file and offers to move it into a secret.
- **The trust map** **(proposed)**: a drawing of the people you have met, with their photos, solid where both confirmed and dashed where one side only.
- **The same vaults on every device** **(unverified)**: vault keys in iCloud Keychain, one item each, so an iPhone, iPad and Mac open the same vaults with nothing to set up.
- **Secrets as files in vaults** **(unverified)**: each entry one encrypted JSON file, behind Face ID, with a strong-password maker.
- **Questions for the owner, by voice** **(unverified)**: the people building the app ask, and the owner answers by choosing, typing or speaking.

articles.markdown:
A research brief written for the [secrets manager design](https://ios.app.voicedebrief.ai/sgit-app/secrets/index.html) on 14 November 2026, by a research agent working from public sources. **Treat prices as approximate** (most come from aggregator sites that disagree), and anything marked *(judgement)* as opinion. It is input to the design, not a decision: the owner decides, through the questions in the app and on the design page.

Date: 14 November 2026. Prices move often and many figures below come from aggregators; check vendor pages before quoting them. Anything marked *(judgement)* is my opinion, not a sourced fact.

## 1. The field, 2025 to 2026

| Product | Sync | Sharing | Trust and identity | Passkeys | Pricing shape | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1Password | Vendor cloud | Shared vaults, organisation accounts | Vendor account plus Secret Key; the vendor directory supplies members' public keys | Yes; exports through Credential Exchange on iOS | Personal, Families, Teams, Business seats | Polish, Secret Key design | Subscription only, cloud only |
| Bitwarden | Vendor cloud or self-hosted | Organisations and collections; a free organisation holds 2 people | Vendor account; the server supplies members' keys | Yes; early adopter of iOS 26 export | Free, Premium, Families (6 people, about $3.99 a month), Teams and Enterprise per seat | Open source, cheap | Several malicious-server attacks found in 2026 |
| Apple Passwords | iCloud Keychain | Shared Groups; owner adds members; an item lives in one group | Apple Account | Native | Free | Built in, zero setup | Apple-only; no permissions; people removed may keep what they saw |
| Proton Pass | Vendor cloud | Shared vaults on paid plans | Proton account | Yes | Free, Plus, Family, Business | Privacy brand, low price | Younger product, fewer team controls |
| Keeper | Vendor cloud | Shared folders with permissions | Vendor account | Yes | Limited free tier, Family about $3.83 a month, Business | Enterprise compliance | Upselling, add-on pricing |
| Dashlane | Vendor cloud | Sharing and groups | Vendor account | Yes | Mostly paid; sources disagree on whether a free tier remains | Clean business admin | Malicious-server findings, price |
| KeePassXC / Strongbox | A file; you choose the sync (Dropbox, iCloud, WebDAV) | Share the file and its password | None: whoever holds the file and password | Strongbox yes; KeePassXC has some | Free / freemium or lifetime | No vendor, open format | Sharing and merge conflicts left to the user |
| Doppler | SaaS | Projects and environments | Org SSO | n/a | Free tier, then per seat | Developer experience | Proprietary, SaaS only |
| Infisical | SaaS or self-hosted | Projects, machine identities | Org accounts, machine identities | n/a | MIT core, Pro priced by identity | Open core, self-host | Org-first, needs an admin |
| HashiCorp Vault | Self-hosted or HCP | Policies | Auth backends, tokens | n/a | BSL 1.1 since 2023; OpenBao is the MPL fork | Power, dynamic secrets | Heavy to run, licence worry |
| 1Password Secrets Automation | Vendor cloud | Service accounts, Connect server | 1Password org | n/a | Part of business plans | Same store for people and machines | Tied to a 1Password business account |

Common thread: all but KeePass rely on an **account with a company** for identity, and "end-to-end" sharing means the vendor's server hands you the other person's public key, the weakness the 2026 ETH Zurich study used. *(judgement)*

Sources: [Bitwarden pricing summary](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/bitwarden-pricing-plans-free-vs-paid-2026-guide), [Apple Shared Groups guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/passwords/mchlc00a3602), [Keeper pricing](https://password-manager.cybernews.com/keeper-password-manager-review/keeper-pricing/), [Infisical on pricing](https://infisical.com/blog/secrets-manager-pricing), [Vault licensing](https://guptadeepak.com/tools/alternatives-to-hashicorp-vault/), [Bitwarden on passkey portability](https://bitwarden.com/blog/security-vendors-join-forces-to-make-passkeys-more-portable-for-everyone/).

## 2. Recurring pain points

- **Breaches have a long tail.** Vaults stolen from LastPass in 2022 were still being cracked in 2025; TRM Labs traced about $35m in crypto thefts to them, and the UK ICO fined LastPass £1.2m. URLs were stored unencrypted, which told attackers which vaults were worth cracking. ([The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2025/12/lastpass-2022-breach-led-to-years-long.html), [Infosecurity](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/experts-trace-35m-stolen-crypto/))
- **"Zero knowledge" is only as good as the server's honesty.** ETH Zurich and USI showed 25 or more attacks against Bitwarden, LastPass and Dashlane under a malicious server, grouped under recovery, key escrow, **sharing** and legacy crypto. ([IACR ePrint 2026/058](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/058), [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/study-uncovers-25-password-recovery.html))
- **Family and small-team sharing.** Free tiers stop at two people (Bitwarden); Apple's groups have no roles beyond owner and member, and Apple warns that people you remove may keep what they saw. ([Apple](https://support.apple.com/guide/passwords/mchlc00a3602), [TWiT](https://twit.tv/posts/tech/apples-passwords-app-enough))
- **Lock-in and passkey portability.** Passkeys were stuck in one manager until FIDO's Credential Exchange. Apple shipped it in iOS 26, but CXF is a standard while the CXP transport was still a draft in mid 2026, and desktop support is patchy. ([Corbado](https://www.corbado.com/blog/ios-26-passkeys.md), [analysis](https://www.youngju.dev/transcribe/2026-07-16-passkey-credential-exchange-half-shipped.en))
- **Trust networks fail open.** The 2019 SKS attack flooded two people's PGP certificates with about 150,000 signatures because anyone could sign anyone. ([Hansen](https://gist.github.com/rjhansen/67ab921ffb4084c865b3618d6955275f))
- **Developers and agents.** GitGuardian counted about 28.65 million new secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025, AI-service secrets up 81%, and over 24,000 in MCP config files; more than 60% of secrets found in 2022 still worked in 2025. ([Help Net Security](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/14/gitguardian-ai-agents-credentials-leak/), [GitGuardian](https://blog.gitguardian.com/ai-secrets-spread-fast/))
- **Onboarding and recovery** are where people give up and where security weakens; recovery is the ETH paper's first category. *(judgement)*

## 3. Ten things SGit Vaults could do better

Ranked by value to a team of 5 to 20, weighted by how directly the architecture gives it. *(judgement)*

1. **A team with no admin and no company account.** *Value:* five people are sharing within ten minutes, with no sign-up, invoice or IT person. *Why possible:* identity is a key pair and membership is a confirmed link, not a row in a vendor database. *Risk:* nobody is in charge when someone leaves or loses a phone.
2. **Sharing that a dishonest server cannot redirect.** *Value:* you know the key you seal to belongs to the person you met. *Why possible:* keys come from cards confirmed in person, never from the server, which shuts out the key-substitution sharing attacks in the ETH study. *Risk:* people skip the confirmation step if it feels like work.
3. **Secrets for agents, scoped and visible.** *Value:* hand an AI session one API key for one job, not a `.env` file. *Why possible:* agents have keys and append lanes, so a secret is a sealed message to that agent alone. *Risk:* an agent that leaks it still leaks it; you need expiry and rotation reminders.
4. **Signed history of every change.** *Value:* "who changed the router password, and when?" has an answer, and you can roll back. *Why possible:* signed commits are the storage model, not an audit add-on. *Risk:* history also keeps old secrets, so rotation must be explained clearly.
5. **No lock-in.** *Value:* leave, self-host or keep several remotes without asking anyone. *Why possible:* local first, server holds only ciphertext, open format. *Risk:* "where is my data?" becomes a question users must understand.
6. **Ask for a secret from someone outside the team.** *Value:* a contractor drops the Wi-Fi or AWS key into your inbox; no shared document, no chat log. *Why possible:* the append lane is write-only, so the sender gets no read access. *Risk:* spam and floods, so lanes need limits and easy rotation; the sender still needs something that can seal (the app or a small web page), which must be built.
7. **Rotation on a branch.** *Value:* change a production key, test it, then merge, so the team is never half on old and half on new. *Why possible:* branches and merges are native. *Risk:* too developer-flavoured for families; hide it there.
8. **Recovery through people you trust.** *Value:* lose every device and get back in with help from three of five confirmed contacts, no vendor reset. *Why possible:* confirmed contacts and sealed messages already exist; key shares are just more sealed messages. *Risk:* hard to get right; a mistake here undoes the whole security story.
9. **A breach of the server reveals almost nothing.** *Value:* no LastPass-style list of which sites you use. *Why possible:* objects are encrypted, including names and URLs. *Risk:* sizes, timing and who talks to whom still leak; say so plainly.
10. **On-device help.** *Value:* sort an import, spot a key pasted into a note, explain a change in plain words, with nothing sent to a cloud. *Why possible:* Apple's on-device models only. *Risk:* small models make mistakes; keep them suggesting, never deciding.

Honest limit: removing a member means new vault keys *and* changing the secrets they saw.

## 4. iOS platform facts that constrain it

- **AutoFill Credential Provider extension.** Subclass `ASCredentialProviderViewController` in an extension and add the `com.apple.developer.authentication-services.autofill-credential-provider` entitlement to **both** the extension and the app ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/ascredentialproviderviewcontroller)). Declare capabilities in the extension's Info.plist under `NSExtension > NSExtensionAttributes > ASCredentialProviderExtensionCapabilities`: `ProvidesPasswords`, `ProvidesPasskeys`, and optionally `ProvidesOneTimeCodes` and `ProvidesTextToInsert` ([Apple forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/745587)).
- **Passkeys in a third-party provider (iOS 17+).** `prepareCredentialList(for:requestParameters:)` for sign-in, `prepareInterface(forPasskeyRegistration:)` for creating a passkey, and `ASPasskeyCredentialIdentity` in `ASCredentialIdentityStore` for QuickType suggestions. Early iOS 17 had bugs, fixed by 17.4 ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/ascredentialproviderviewcontroller/prepareinterface(forpasskeyregistration:)), [forum](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/747286)). The provider stores the passkey's private key itself.
- **iOS 18 and later** add one-time codes (`prepareOneTimeCodeCredentialList`), text insertion, and conditional (automatic) passkey upgrade (`performWithoutUserInteractionIfPossible(passkeyRegistration:)`). The latest SDK also adds save and generate password requests and the `report...` signals from sites. **iOS 26** adds Credential Exchange import and export (`ASCredentialExportManager`) ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/ascredentialproviderviewcontroller), [Corbado](https://www.corbado.com/blog/wwdc25-passkeys-os26.md)).
- **Face ID.** `LocalAuthentication` (`LAContext`) or a keychain item protected by `SecAccessControl` with a biometry flag; the app must set `NSFaceIDUsageDescription`.
- **Secure Enclave.** It holds P-256 keys only and they never leave the device. The signing key could live there per device; RSA-4096 cannot, so it must be wrapped by an enclave key or stored as an ordinary keychain item. *(design consequence, my judgement)*
- **iCloud Keychain sync.** `kSecAttrSynchronizable` items cannot use any `...ThisDeviceOnly` accessibility value or `kSecAttrAccess` ([Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/ksecattrsynchronizable), [Apple](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/ksecattraccessible)). Syncing keys there makes Apple's account a recovery path.
- **App Groups and keychain sharing.** The extension runs in its own process, so vault files go in a shared App Group container and keys in a shared keychain access group (`keychain-access-groups`). The extension should read a small index, not a whole vault, as extensions get less memory. *(judgement)*
- **Needs the account holder (or an Admin) in the developer portal:** an App ID for the extension, the AutoFill Credential Provider capability on both App IDs, the App Group and keychain group registered, and new provisioning profiles. A Mac build needs the same on the macOS side.

## 5. First-run and team storyboard

**One person alone**
1. Welcome: "Your secrets, in vaults only you can open." One button.
2. Face ID consent; keys generated on the device (show it happening, a few seconds).
3. Your card: name and a photo you take now. Explain that the photo helps friends know it is you.
4. First vault created locally; offer to import (Apple Passwords, 1Password, Bitwarden, CSV, Credential Exchange on iOS 26).
5. Turn on AutoFill: `ASSettingsHelper` opens the right Settings page.
6. Optional: add a remote server. Optional: recovery later, when you have contacts.

**Two people meeting**

7. "Add someone": both open a QR screen. A scans B.
8. A sees B's card with **B's photo**, takes a quick photo of the person in front of them, and compares. "Is this the person in front of you?"
9. Both phones show the same short safety code (six words or digits). Both say it aloud and tap Confirm. A link exists only when **both** confirm.
10. Remote fallback: card sent over a messenger, confirmed by video call with the same code. Mark it "confirmed remotely".

**A group of five**

11. One person starts "New team" and shows one QR; others scan it and each card appears in a grid with photos.
12. Each pair that has not confirmed yet gets a tick to do; the app shows who is still unconfirmed. A shared vault can include only people the creator has confirmed. *(judgement: do not let trust pass through others)*
13. Name the team vault, pick members, done; each member's copy of the key is sealed to their key.
14. Offer recovery: "Choose three of these four to help you get back in."

## 6. Decisions for the product owner

1. **Is iCloud Keychain allowed to hold keys?** Recommend: no for identity and vault keys by default; offer it as an opt-in recovery aid with a clear warning.
2. **How do people recover after losing every device?** Recommend: social recovery through confirmed contacts (threshold such as three of five), plus a printed recovery sheet. No vendor reset, ever.
3. **Must every team member confirm every other member?** Recommend: the vault creator must have confirmed each member; members need not confirm each other to read, but must to share onward.
4. **Is AutoFill (passwords and passkeys) in version one?** Recommend: yes for passwords and passkeys; it is the daily habit that keeps people in the app. Leave one-time codes and text insertion for later.
5. **What does removing a member do?** Recommend: re-key the vault automatically, then show a checklist of the secrets that person saw, with "rotate" actions. Never imply removal un-shares the past.
